newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil deputy says Motta gave him TV rights - paper.
newsitem.headline: Brazil deputy says Motta gave him TV rights - paper.

text.p: A Brazilian deputy who was allegedly paid off for his vote in Congress by two governors and Communications Minister Sergio Motta allegedly was also granted a television concession by Motta, a newspaper reported Thursday.

News of the vote-buying scandal in which five deputies were allegedly paid to vote in favor of a bill allowing President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to stand for re-election first broke on Tuesday in the Folha de Sao Paulo newspaper. It reported on Wednesday that there were indications Motta allegedly could have supplied the money.
Motta denied any role in the vote-buying scheme.

On Thursday, Folha de Sao Paulohird exclusive story since Tuesd said it obtained secretly taped telephone conversations in which Deputy Ronivon Santiago purportedly says Motta also granted him a concession to run a television station.
"I was there with Sergio Motta. You know I'm getting a television, channel 40," Folha quoted Santiago as saying.
In the same telephone conversation with an unidentified third person, Santiago allegedly also speaks of a concession for a radio station which Motta has promised to grant him.

Santiago purportedly said the TV concession was registered in the name of a friend, former taxi driver Valcy de Souza Campos, but Campos denies he is Motta's frontman, saying the TV station belongs to him alone, according to Folha.

News of Motta's alleged involvement in the cash-for-votes scheme unsettled financial markets Wednesday with shares on the Sao Paulo stock exchange falling 3.43 percent and Brazilian Brady debt declining for the second day running.
However, the government says the scandal poses no threat to Brazil's economy, and analysts are suggesting a wait-and-see approach.

The re-election bill, which would allow presidents, state governors and mayors to run for a second consecutive term, was approved in January in the Chamber of Deputies in what was considered the biggest test to date of Cardoso's administration.
The bill is now in the Senate where the first of two full votes is expected to take place next week.
Cardoso, who hopes to become Brazil's first re-elected president next year, urged Congress to investigate quickly the reports which, he said, took him by surprise.
The scandal comes at a delicate time for Cardoso who is trying to overcome resistance in Congress to his civil service and pension reforms.
An internal congressional inquiry was launched Tuesday and has seven days to investigate the allegations. The probe could lead to suspension of the lawmakers involved in the alleged scam.

Left-wing opposition parties said they were close to gathering enough signatures in the lower house to set up a wide ranging Commission of Parliamentary Inquiry (CPI) into the scandal. They also demanded the re-election bill be put on hold.
"There is nothing that places at risk the outlook for the country's economy," said presidential spokesman Sergio Amaral.
Motta, a close friend and business partner of Cardoso, denied any role in the scandal.
"I reject and do not recognize any of the statements transcribed in the Folha de Sao Paulo," he told reporters Wednesday. "There's not one solid accusation or fact."
The minister also said he would be taking legal steps to oblige the deputies quoted by the newspaper to either confirm or deny the comments attributed to them.
((--Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 507 4151))
